repos.title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
repos.paper_summary: OpenVLHarness is a multimodal tool-use harness for MLLMs, built around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer wraps heterogeneous perception, search, and computation tools behind task-level interfaces and renders their outputs into model-readable observations. Memory registers images, structured data, and web references under handles, and a Python Coding Agent runs generated programs over stored values, so later steps can reuse earlier evidence. The harness is evaluated on 22 benchmarks across four domains with eight backbones. Averaged over the 22 datasets, it raises Qwen3-VL-8B from 34.2 to 45.4 and Qwen3-VL-32B from 38.3 to 50.9, outperforming OctoTools and Visual Sketchpad. With GPT-6 Luna at medium effort, it scores 56.5 against 45.8 for the base model, and it is reported to outperform Codex and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort while using at most 37% of their model-token cost. Qwen3-VL results are means of three seeds; GPT-6 results are single runs, so their variance is unreported in the main table. The paper's benchmark-level gains are uneven, with some datasets, such as V* for Qwen3-VL-8B, showing no gain.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Extra reasoning budget gives diminishing returns, so the paper proposes OpenVLHarness to add multimodal evidence acquisition.

digest_headlines.heading: Harness Design
digest_headlines.headline: OpenVLHarness pairs a capability layer that renders tool outputs with persistent memory of handle-addressed artifacts.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: OpenVLHarness raises Qwen3-VL-8B scores on 22 benchmarks, for example from 32.00 to 48.56 on a counting benchmark.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior visual tool-use systems use fixed plans or task-specific frameworks, while this paper keeps multimodal artifacts addressable across turns.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Released harness gives broad gains on 22 benchmarks and can specialize to domains without updating model weights.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix reports tool-call volume, capability distribution, paired accuracy effects, and object-count distributions of benchmarks.

repos.title: Möbius: A Unified Motion-Language Model Bridging Understanding and Generation
repos.paper_summary: Möbius is a unified motion-language model that runs the full motion diffusion process inside the same multimodal attention space as text and motion understanding, rather than conditioning an external diffusion module on language-model features. It operates on continuous frame-level raw motion (D=201) with no discrete tokenizer or pretrained motion VAE. Training is two-stage: motion captioning first, then generation with the understanding parameters frozen. On HumanML3D text-to-motion, Möbius-0.6B reports R@1 0.821 and FID 6.13, versus 0.671 and 21.0 for MotionGPT3, the strongest unified baseline in Table 1. The 1.7B variant, trained on 1,700 hours of motion data, reports FID 10.7. Motion captioning (Table 2) reports BLEU-4 0.203 for the 0.6B model against 0.161 for MotionGPT3. On MotionFix editing, the 0.6B variant with additional MotionFix data reports FID 0.0955 against 0.134 for MotionLab. Limitations stated by the authors: experiments cover only controlled single-person motion, with multi-person interaction, detailed hand motion, and retargeting left to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Möbius runs the entire motion diffusion process inside the shared multimodal space used for understanding, not an external module.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior unified motion models either tokenize motion or hand language features to an external diffusion module.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Möbius uses raw frame-level motion with role-specific parameters and shared attention, trained understanding-first.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Möbius-0.6B scores 0.8209 on top-1 retrieval and 6.1291 on Fréchet distance, ahead of unified baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude the shared space works at 1.7B scale, with evidence limited to controlled single-person motion.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists datasets, architecture and training settings, task construction, inference settings, timing, evaluation protocols, and extra completion results.

repos.title: Making Images Real Again: A Comprehensive Survey on Deep Image Composition
repos.paper_summary:
This paper surveys deep image composition, a task that combines foreground and background images to produce realistic composites. It decomposes the problem into sub-tasks: object placement, image blending, image harmonization, shadow generation, reflection generation, and generative composition. The authors categorize methods for each sub-task into traditional rule-based approaches and deep learning techniques, such as GANs and diffusion models. They also summarize available datasets and evaluation metrics, including FID, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and user studies.

The paper releases `libcom`, a Python toolbox assembling over 10 functions for these tasks, and an online workbench. Experimental comparisons are provided on specific datasets like OPA (73,470 images) for object placement and iHarmony4 for harmonization. For instance, in object placement, discriminative approaches like FOPA outperform generative ones like PlaceNet. In painterly harmonization, diffusion-based methods like PHDiffusion outperform GAN-based baselines on challenging textures. Limitations include the high cost of collecting paired ground-truth data for harmonization and the difficulty of evaluating arbitrary compositions without dense annotations.

repos.title: WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One Agent From Narration to Long-Form Video
repos.paper_summary: WeVisCut is a script-to-video system that pairs a stateful tool harness with a single 9B policy trained on executable editing traces. The harness tracks shared production state, validates tool calls, and returns typed blockers that the policy can act on. Editing inversion, verified replay, observe–reflect–repair, and trajectory materialization turn 3,750 finished Bilibili videos into 134,771 training examples. The Qwen3.5-9B policy is trained with LoRA SFT, runtime-verified rejection-sampled fine-tuning, Guided-OPD, and RCF-DAPO, which compares rewards only within matched roles and contexts. On a 100-task benchmark scored with five metrics over five runs, it improves its base model by 16.0 points in Overall Score and reaches comparable performance to Claude Opus 5 with nearly 33× fewer generated tokens per successful output minute. It also outperforms task-matched native editors, Crayotter and VideoAgent, under a shared tool environment. Stated limitations: broader template coverage and more reliable retrieval are needed, and Overall Score has no uncertainty estimate.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: WeVisCut couples a stateful script-to-video harness with executable data and one 9B policy for narrated long-form video.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work contrasts WeVisCut with tool-agent training, video editing agents, and evaluations that do not link scripts, traces, and renders.

digest_headlines.heading: WeVisCut Agent Framework
digest_headlines.headline: A shared policy chooses tools over a stateful runtime that validates calls, keeps artifacts, and repairs shots before delivery.

digest_headlines.heading: Data Construction
digest_headlines.headline: Four-stage pipeline recovers editing intent from finished videos and replays it to produce executable training examples.

digest_headlines.heading: Training WeVisCut
digest_headlines.headline: Three phases train the policy by imitation, recovery learning on policy-reached states, and decision optimization within matched roles.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On 100 held-out tasks, WeVisCut reaches 90.5 Overall Score, close to Claude Opus 5 at 89.9, with far fewer generated tokens.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The trained 9B policy improves all five metrics over its base model and approaches Claude Opus 5 at lower generation cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists admission rules for replayed training data, loss and intervention schedules, reward formulas, evaluation protocol, and a sample trace.

repos.title: ODE Policy: Robot Learning via Action Dynamics, Not Actions
repos.paper_summary: ODE policy learns the dynamics of a robot action, modeling the policy as a neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) whose vector field is conditioned on the observation. Each action is integrated from the previous one at inference, so the executed trajectory is continuous by construction. In imitation learning, the field is trained by matching integrated action chunks to demonstrations, and a contractive perturbation of chunk start points pulls states back toward the demonstrations. An optional diversity head supports multi-modal behavior. On LIBERO, it reaches 79.2% success after one epoch, against at most 43.2% for baselines. As the action head of π0.5, it reaches 96.0% against 75.5% for flow matching. It generates a chunk 10.8 times faster than flow matching in simulation. It has the highest success rate on all 14 real-world tasks. As the actor of SuperMimic in RL, it ends training with a return of 0.885 against 0.845. Limitations: encoding the binary gripper command as a field state lowers LIBERO success after one epoch from 79.2% to 74.5%. Early model-free RL experiments showed little gain and sometimes a loss. Several analyses use a single seed.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Most robot policies map observations to discrete actions and leave continuity to be learned; ODE policy instead learns the action's dynamics.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior ODE robot policies fix the vector field's form, and efficiency methods keep direct-action actors, which ODE policy changes.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: Direct-action policies output each action separately, while a neural ODE defines a field integrated over time.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method integrates a learned action field over each chunk, trains it on integrated paths, and adds a sampled diversity offset.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: The evaluation compares ODE policy with 14 baselines on simulated and real tasks, with shared backbones, data, and training schedules.

digest_headlines.heading: Simulation Results
digest_headlines.headline: In simulation, ODE policy learns faster, needs fewer demonstrations, generates actions faster, and keeps multiple behavior modes.

digest_headlines.heading: Real-World Results
digest_headlines.headline: On four real robots, ODE policy has the highest success rate on each reported task and transfers dexterous skills across labs.

digest_headlines.heading: Ablation Studies
digest_headlines.headline: Ablations show that chunking is essential and that removing the contractive perturbation drops the one-epoch success rate from 79.8% to 58.4%.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Future Directions
digest_headlines.headline: Discussion argues continuity built into the policy improves efficiency across scales and suggests three preliminary extensions.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists benchmark and robot details, training settings, timing tables, and extra generalization, multi-modal, and ablation results.

repos.title: Fewer Tokens, Better Action: GPT-6 Astra Robot Agents with 14% Higher Success Rate but 65% Fewer Tokens
repos.paper_summary:
PyRUA-Lean is an interactive code-execution framework for vision-language model (VLM) robot agents that reduces token overhead while improving task success. The agent generates Python cells that compose classical robot primitives and learned vision-language-action policies, executing conditional checks and local retries within the runtime. Only explicitly requested images and state feedback are returned to the VLM for replanning, whereas intermediate results remain in a persistent program state.

Across 700 simulated task instances from LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboCasa365, PyRUA-Lean increases overall success from 63.1% to 71.7% compared to a tool-calling baseline using the same GPT-6 Astra planner. On instances solved by both agents, it uses 49% fewer LLM calls and 65% fewer input tokens, reducing estimated cost per episode from USD 1.63 to USD 0.74. Ablations show these gains persist without VLA policies or operating guides. Limitations include evaluation restricted to simulation with one run per instance, and efficiency gains diminish on tasks dominated by VLA policies where initial prompts account for much of the input cost.

repos.title: ReLift: Dense 3D Tracking as Lifted Trajectory Repair
repos.paper_summary: ReLift is a feed-forward method for dense monocular 3D point tracking that repairs and completes trajectories lifted from pretrained 2D trackers and depth and camera models. Each 2D track is lifted along its viewing ray using the estimated range, and occluded observations are masked and filled by linear interpolation. A corrector alternates attention along each track with attention across tracks within each temporal chunk, and predicts per-frame XYZ residuals that are added to the lift. It trains only on clean PointOdyssey trajectories with randomized corruptions of ray direction, range, drift, and occlusion dropouts, so no tracker, depth model, or renderer runs during training. The same weights, without retraining, improve all six tracker–geometry pairings tested. On WorldTrack, ReLift reports the highest mean APD3D, improving on the strongest baselines by 2.1 on all points and 3.0 on dynamic points. Its faster configurations run 2.7–4.4× faster than 4RC. Limitations: accuracy remains sensitive to input geometry, and the simulated errors omit camera-pose errors and persistent identity switches.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Monocular dense 3D tracking can focus learning on repair and completion because pretrained 2D trackers and geometry models already handle correspondence and depth.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior methods fit 3D tracks with per-scene optimization or learn them feed-forward, while ReLift reuses 2D tracks and frozen geometry.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A trajectory corrector alternates temporal and across-track attention to predict 3D residuals on lifted trajectories.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On WorldTrack, the corrector with CoWTracker and 4RC geometry reaches 89.01 mean all-point accuracy, above 4RC's 86.94.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Performance still depends on input geometry, and handling persistent correspondence errors is left to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists preprocessing, architecture, training corruptions, evaluation protocol, baseline configurations and runtime measurements.

repos.title: Evolving Agent Teams
repos.paper_summary: Evolving Agent Teams is a multi-agent framework for open-ended code optimization. A supervisor agent restructures the team's roles, coordination, and knowledge management when a run plateaus, instead of keeping a fixed configuration. A persistent file system holds a learnings document, an evolution history, and per-team artifacts, so each new team inherits prior results. The supervisor runs when a team finishes or on a fixed-interval cron job. Workers are Claude Code agents on Claude Opus 4.6. On GPU kernel tasks, the framework outperforms Claude Code under a matched token budget. On MLA paged decode over 47 FlashInfer-Bench workloads on H100, Claude Code plateaus at 0.44–0.51× of the FlashInfer baseline, and the evolving team reaches 0.75×. With extended budget, it reaches 1.21× mean speedup and is faster on 36 of 47 workloads. Ablations give 0.31× for a fixed four-role team and 0.28× for Codex (GPT-5.5 xhigh). Each main setting was run twice and ablations once, which limits statistical comparisons. The paper also lists a missing cost-versus-performance analysis as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing coding agents stall at local optima on expert-written GPU kernels, so the paper evolves the agent team during optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work mostly fixes agent roles or uses population search; this work restructures one team under a persistent supervisor.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A supervisor diagnoses each plateau, rewrites roles, coordination, and knowledge management, with a persistent file system carrying experience across teams.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: At matched budget the evolving team beats Claude Code on the four tasks, and reaches 1.21× on MLA decode with extra budget.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Evolving teams surpass FlashInfer MLA decode at 1.21× mean speedup; two runs per main setting limit statistical comparisons.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: The work was done at the Sky Computing Lab, with compute support from SemiAnalysis, Amazon, AMD, and NVIDIA.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists supervisor-invented roles, a slow-start case study, extra settings, and matched-budget solo ablations.

repos.title: Matrix-Game 4.0: Harnessing Video Models for Real-Time Playable Game Worlds
repos.paper_summary:
Matrix-Game 4.0 is a real-time game-world system that separates game execution from visual generation. A lightweight engine keeps world state and enforces rules, a coding agent turns player requests into game code and captions, and an autoregressive video renderer turns low-poly proxy frames into detailed 480p frames.

The renderer adapts Wan2.2 5B to video-to-video generation. It is conditioned on the proxy, a per-frame caption built from engine state, reference frames, and the first frame. It is trained on 114,334 paired UE5 clips (1,712 hours), then distilled into a causal generator that produces four-frame chunks in one or two denoising steps.

On one RTX 5090 at 480p, the paper reports 60 FPS gameplay, 112 ms key-press-to-display latency, and 83 FPS single-step steady-state throughput with 18.2 GiB peak memory. Against the unoptimized causal baseline (4.5 FPS, 1110 ms), the cumulative optimizations give 19× throughput and 9.9× lower latency. The latency figure applies only to the evaluated configuration. The authors list lower inference cost, visual fidelity, higher-resolution refinement, and multiplayer rendering as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Playable worlds need persistent state, executable rules and low latency, which motivates separating game logic from video generation.

digest_headlines.heading: Roadmap
digest_headlines.headline: A game engine, a coding agent and a video model form a harness, with the engine holding world state and enforcing rules.

digest_headlines.heading: Data
digest_headlines.headline: Paired Unreal Engine captures of low-poly and high-fidelity video give 114,334 training clips across four scene types.

digest_headlines.heading: Rendering Model
digest_headlines.headline: A video model is distilled into a causal generator that denoises each four-frame chunk in one or two steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Real-Time Inference
digest_headlines.headline: Cumulative optimizations raise steady-state throughput from 4.5 to 83.4 FPS and cut latency from 1110 ms to 112 ms.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Visual results are qualitative only, but Matrix-Game 4.0 reports the lowest latency among four compared systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior interactive models keep dynamics in the network, while several recent systems assign rules to code and render with video.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: The harness design is offered as a reusable foundation, with lower inference cost and hardware needs left as near-term work.

repos.title: Wave Forcing: Towards Speed-of-Light Streaming Video Generation
repos.paper_summary: Wave Forcing (WF) is a chunk-wise autoregressive method for streaming video generation that starts the next video chunk's denoising before the previous chunk finishes. Each denoising stage and a cache-refresh stage run on separate full-model replicas, so one completed chunk emerges per forward round after pipeline fill. Chunk-wise causal attention lets newer chunks read earlier, cleaner chunks. A three-stage training recipe (mixed-noise distribution-matching distillation, teacher-guided motion supervision with LPIPS, and on-policy adaptation with self-generated history) adapts Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B to this context. The Wave Runtime implements early K/V delivery and communication-computation overlap. On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, 5-step WF reaches a VBench Total of 81.64 versus 81.15 for Rolling Forcing, and Dynamic Degree rises from 51.39 to 94.44 on short videos. 4-step WF reaches 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs, a 7.07× speedup over a 19.06-FPS single-GPU baseline. Across six model scales (1.3B–14B), Wave Parallelism reaches 1.025–2.530× the throughput of the faster context-parallel baseline under Sage+W8A8. Limitations: VBench does not capture long-stream subject loss or camera drift, so the paper adds Subject Preservation and Camera Drift on a 100-prompt subset. Aggregate timings do not isolate VAE bottlenecks, and the gap to context parallelism narrows at 14B.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Wave Forcing targets one chunk per forward round and reports 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: Sequential chunk generation needs S denoising forwards plus one store forward, so even one-step denoising takes two passes.

digest_headlines.heading: Wave Forcing
digest_headlines.headline: Chunk-wise causal attention lets newer chunks read earlier, cleaner chunks before those finish denoising.

digest_headlines.heading: Wave Runtime
digest_headlines.headline: Wave Runtime publishes key-value data early from stage-owned replicas, overlapping transfers with computation to cut waits.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Five-step Wave Forcing scores 81.64 VBench Total against 81.15 for Rolling Forcing, with higher motion and subject retention.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans streaming video training, blockwise diffusion in language and robotics, and parallel execution baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Subject and drift diagnostics rely on a 100-prompt subset, and output-path decoding capacity remains unresolved.

digest_headlines.heading: Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Future work targets end-to-end profiling, mid-generation prompt changes, and interactive world models, none yet evaluated.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Jointly designing context, training, and execution yields one chunk per forward round after fill with comparable overall quality.

digest_headlines.heading: AI Use Statement
digest_headlines.headline: AI assistants supported framing, organization, editing, and figure work, and the authors remain responsible for the claims.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists training schedules and loss details, runtime buffer and cache semantics, the same-graph proof, parameter configurations, and extended future work.
